title: Runtime Moderation Architecture and Latency Tradeoffs
summary: Deep technical discussion about where to place safety filters in the inference stack for a VPC/on-prem deployment, quantization and KV cache interactions with moderation, and batching/throughput impacts. We explored inline vs post-processing filters, lightweight prefilters, async moderation patterns, and fallbacks for capacity degradation. Agreed to run controlled microbenchmarks on their infra and follow up with suggested configs and a benchmark spreadsheet.
transcript:
Header: 2025-05-08 15:00 UTC | Duration 55m | Recording: on
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Cole (Redwood SE), Marisol Nguyen (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (ClearHarbor), Paul Becker (ClearHarbor), Rita Gomez (ClearHarbor)

[00:00] Samira: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, can you all hear me?
[00:02] Aisha: Yep, loud and clear. Thanks for squeezing us in.
[00:06] Samira: Awesome. Quick agenda — Ethan is going to walk through tradeoffs for running moderation in-line on the serving path versus as a post-process or async pipeline. We'll also cover KV cache impacts, batching, and what changes when you're in a VPC/on-prem environment.
[00:18] Ethan: Cool. I'll start with a quick mental model. When we say "in-line" moderation we mean the filter executes during token generation or immediately at end-of-response before returning tokens to the client. "Post-process" is a separate step after the response has been produced, either on another service or a worker pool.
[00:34] Paul: Right, and for us in healthcare anything that touches PHI has to be fully auditable and can't go to third-party moderation services, so in-line on-prem is the safe default, but we worry about latency.
[00:45] Ethan: Totally. There are three axes to watch: latency tail, throughput or cost, and correctness / recall of the safety classifier. In-line gives the best correctness because you can stop generation early and avoid sending sensitive tokens over the wire, but it increases p99 latency because the moderation check is in the critical path.
[01:02] Rita: Can you quantify p99 impacts? ballpark.
[01:05] Ethan: Depends on model size and whether your classifier runs on GPU. Example: running a lightweight transformer-based classifier on the same GPU adds ~30-80ms per request in our benchmarks for mid-sized models; running on CPU can add 100-300ms depending on CPU tier and concurrent load. If you batch classifiers you can amortize cost but that increases latency for single requests.
[01:23] Aisha: We typically target 200ms p95 for conversational ops. If in-line adds 80ms that's acceptable; p99 is tougher.
[01:30] Marisol: One hybrid approach we recommend: a shallow prefilter inline — a tiny logistic or distilled classifier that flags likely-sensitive outputs quickly, then stream tokens to client while simultaneously enqueuing the full response for a stronger post-process check. If the post-check flips the verdict to "block", you can retract or send a correction via follow-up message. This reduces initial latency impact.
[01:52] Paul: Retracting is messy for UX though. We build front-ends that can't show PHI, so a retract would be jarring.
[01:58] Ethan: Agreed. For strict UX constraints, keep the final moderation decision before the client sees content — so either full in-line or do synchronous post-processing before delivering. The tradeoff then is throughput and cost.
[02:12] Aisha: How does KV cache factor into this? If we cache prefixes, could a cached continuation bypass checks?
[02:18] Ethan: Good question. KV cache stores past key/values for fast autoregressive decoding. If you serve cached continuations, you still need to run moderation on the reconstructed output. The danger is when you have a prefix that was previously deemed safe and you reuse it to generate new content — the new continuation could go unsafe. So the moderation system must be aware of cache hits: either re-run checks on the concatenated output, or tag cached entries with metadata that forces re-eval when context changes.
[02:43] Rita: Is there a light-weight metadata approach?
[02:45] Marisol: We sometimes attach a safety-vector summary or fingerprint to the cache entry. The vector is cheap (low-dim) and can be quickly checked; if the new prompt would alter the vector beyond a threshold, you force a re-eval. It's not perfect but reduces unnecessary heavyweight checks. Note: imperfect fingerprinting can miss cases, so for regulated use we suggest stricter policies.
[03:04] Aisha: What about quantization? If we've quantized the model to INT8 or lower for cost reasons, does moderation accuracy drop?
[03:11] Ethan: Generally, quantization affects generation quality more than classifier reliability, but if your classifier uses the same quantized model or quantized embeddings, there can be subtle drift. For small distilled classifiers, we usually keep them in FP16 on GPU or float on CPU to avoid calibration issues. If you run the classifier on a quantized path, run evals with your safety test suite — we can help there.
[03:31] Paul: For VPC/on-prem, are there architectural templates? We don't want cross-cloud callbacks for moderation.
[03:37] Samira: Yes, we have a few patterns. Pattern A = fully on-prem: serving runtime + classifier on same hardware, everything inside the VPC, no external calls. Pattern B = hybrid: serve in VPC but push non-PHI moderation telemetry to a managed Redwood service — only if allowed. Pattern C = async out-of-band: serve quickly, store output to an internal queue, run heavy checks on separate cluster, then annotate results in a datastore and trigger app logic.
[04:03] Rita: Pattern C still risks delivery of unsafe content.
[04:06] Ethan: Right, but you can gate delivery by a policy. Example: for low-risk domains, show streaming tokens and mark as provisional; for high-risk intents, require synchronous blocking. Setting those policies requires good intent classification up-front.
[04:22] Aisha: OK. Let's talk numbers. If we put a medium-weight classifier in-line on GPU for us (NVIDIA A10G equiv), what's the QPS impact when doing batching for generation and separate batching for classifiers?
[04:33] Ethan: In our internal tests, for batched generation at batch size 8 on a mid-sized model, you get X gen throughput. Running a classifier inline at per-request time reduces effective QPS by about 10-30% depending on the classifier cost and batching alignment. The biggest inefficiency is when gen batching and classifier batching don't align; you may get smaller classifier batches which are less efficient. The solution is to co-batch: run classifier inference in the same batched window if you can align request windows, but that increases latency for some requests.
[05:02] Paul: Co-batching sounds complex. Any orchestration patterns?
[05:05] Marisol: Use a scheduling window with a 5-15ms micro-batch delay to gather classifier requests into usable batch sizes. That buys throughput at the cost of small added latency — sometimes acceptable. Redwood's runtime supports micro-batching knobs for both generation and auxiliary tasks.
[05:18] Rita: In terms of fallback, if classifier cluster is overloaded what should happen?
[05:22] Ethan: You should have a policy: fail-closed or fail-open. For healthcare, you probably fail-closed meaning block or degrade to a safe canned response. Another option: route to a smaller, cheaper on-host classifier as fallback — distilled model that is conservative (high recall, lower precision) to avoid false negatives.
[05:38] Aisha: How do we keep costs down while maintaining low latency?
[05:40] Ethan: A few levers: 1) use shallow prefilters to avoid heavy post-processing; 2) cache moderation decisions for repeated prompts; 3) co-locate classifier on same GPU to avoid RPC overhead; 4) use mixed-precision FP16 for gen and keep classifier FP16 if validated; 5) intelligent routing — send safety-critical traffic to dedicated low-latency pool, and non-critical to cheaper capacity.
[06:01] Paul: About caching moderation decisions, what keys do you use? prompt hash? user session?
[06:06] Marisol: Typically a hash of the full prompt + user attributes + conversation state fingerprint. Be conservative on TTLs and invalidate on context changes. For example, short TTL for conversational continuations, longer TTL for static content like templates.
[06:20] Aisha: Any gotchas with streaming responses and moderation?
[06:23] Ethan: Streaming complicates things because you might emit early tokens before the final moderation verdict. Approaches: stream provisional tokens with a visible badge; buffer until a safe threshold then stream; or stream only non-sensitive prefixes. For regulated apps we avoid streaming sensitive content until final check.
[06:40] Rita: Could we do a two-tier streaming — initial sanitized gist then follow with full content if safe?
[06:45] Marisol: Yes, that's a workable UX pattern. Send a short summary or redacted version immediately, then deliver full content after checks. It reduces perceived latency.
[06:55] Paul: Do you have example numbers for additional token latency if we add a classifier that runs on CPU and communicates over RPC?
[07:01] Ethan: Another rough: network + RPC overhead typical 5-15ms internal; CPU classification 80-200ms; so you're adding ~100-220ms p95. If you add batching you might reduce per-example cost but add 20-80ms additional wait.
[07:19] Aisha: We want to avoid external callbacks — so everything must stay inside our VPC. Redwood Private is appealing. Does Private support hosting classifier as a service next to runtime?
[07:27] Samira: Yes, Private supports co-deploying auxiliary services. You can run classifiers as sidecar containers or colocated processes. We can provide deployment examples.
[07:33] Paul: What about audit logs and KMS? All moderation decisions must be auditable and encrypted at rest.
[07:39] Ethan: We can write audit logs to a customer-managed store, integrate with your KMS/HSM for encryption. In Private mode, logs never leave your network unless you opt in. We also provide trace IDs you can correlate between generation and moderation events.
[07:53] Rita: Any performance overhead for auditing?
[07:56] Marisol: Minor. Writing JSON logs to a fast local store is ~ms level; if you ship to a remote SIEM there is more latency but it can be async.
[08:04] Aisha: Let's talk about our specific workload: mostly short dialogues, average seq len 120, spike traffic during med triage windows. We need p95 < 300ms.
[08:13] Ethan: For seq len 120, inline shallow classifier on same GPU likely keeps you within p95. For p99 you may need dedicated low-latency pool. Also consider autoscale for burst windows.
[08:26] Paul: We already have a dedicated GPU cluster but with multitenant workloads. Any isolation tips?
[08:31] Ethan: Use capacity pinning for high-priority traffic, use QoS to reserve a fraction of GPU memory and compute. Redwood Dedicated supports node pools and strict tenancy for this.
[08:40] Aisha: Could you walk through a sample decision matrix for inline vs post-process?
[08:45] Ethan: Sure, quick matrix: Critical PHI? -> Yes -> Inline synchronous (fail-closed). Critical latency? -> Yes -> Shallow prefilter + synchronous heavyweight only for flagged. External moderation allowed? -> No -> All in-VPC. High throughput low-risk? -> Post-process async allowed. We can share a one-pager.
[09:01] Marisol: Also include quantization/precision notes: if you quantize heavily, re-eval the safety tests; keep classifier separately tuned.
[09:09] Rita: For our compliance team, we need to see regression tests and sample evaluation sets.
[09:14] Samira: We'll share Redwood's eval harness and you can run it against your classifiers and quantized paths.
[09:19] Aisha: Cool. Any anti-patterns we should avoid?
[09:22] Ethan: One big anti-pattern is assuming a cached prefix implies safety for all continuations — that can silently slip. Another is relying solely on post-process when UX or regulations require pre-delivery guarantees. Also don't conflate token-level filters with intent-level checks; both are needed.
[09:38] Paul: What about model fallbacks — to a smaller model for safety?
[09:41] Marisol: We do fallback routing: if heavy model or classifier saturated, route to a conservative smaller model that has been tuned to avoid risky completions. This reduces quality but keeps you safe and serviceable.
[09:52] Aisha: Let's talk benchmarks — what data points do you recommend we collect in our microbenchmark?
[09:56] Ethan: Collect: per-request latency p50/p95/p99 generation-only; classifier-only latency p50/p95/p99 (CPU and GPU runs); combined end-to-end for inline; throughput at target batch sizes; cache hit ratios and latency for cache hits vs misses; effect of quantization on classifier precision/recall and generation quality; memory/VRAM usage under peak.
[10:19] Paul: We'll run those. Can you share a benchmark spreadsheet template?
[10:22] Samira: Yes, we'll send a template and a recommended config.
[10:25] Rita: Also include a recommended TTL for safety cache.
[10:28] Marisol: For conversational contexts, 30-120s TTLs are common; for templates longer. But depends on your app.
[10:36] Aisha: OK next steps?
[10:38] Samira: I'll capture action items now.
[10:40] Ethan: Action items:
[10:41] Ethan: Ethan: Run an internal microbenchmark on our side to validate the numbers? Sorry, on your side.
[10:44] Paul: Yep.
[10:45] Samira: We'll follow with a recommended config and the benchmark sheet.
[10:47] Marisol: We'll include a sample deployment manifest for Private with classifier as sidecar.
[10:50] Aisha: Timeline? We want initial results in two weeks.
[10:52] Samira: Sounds reasonable. We'll plan to reconvene after your first run.
[10:56] Rita: Also include SOC2 notes for audit and the KMS integration steps.
[10:59] Samira: Will do.
[11:02] Samira: Thanks everyone — we'll send notes and artifacts.
[11:05] Aisha: Thanks all.
[11:07] End of recording.

Notes: transcript contains occasional ASR mistakes e.g., "K-V cash" for KV cache in some places, minor speaker mislabels.
